item.title: China's token prices double, usage triples amid AI application boom: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24 16:57:00
Concept photo of token Photo: VCG Prices for Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) large model token services have doubled from the second half of 2025, while usage amount tripled. The average daily token use reached about 500 trillion in June 2026 - nearly four times the level in December 2025, according to a latest report. Analysts said that the combination of higher prices and sharply higher usage signals that demand for AI models is now strong enough to absorb a price recovery - and that the industry is moving toward competition on service quality. Domestic AI model suppliers continued to roll out more capable models for customers, including Moonshot AI and ByteDance's Volcengine, which released their latest new AI models on Saturday. The report released by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) described the market as rising in both price and volume. The report was motivated in part by the growing number of MaaS (Model as a Service) providers supplying token services through public cloud APIs (application programming interfaces), and by users' lack of intuitive benchmarks for service performance and the resulting difficulty in choosing models. "In other words, a growing number of companies now sell online access to AI models, charging by how much the model is used. But customers have no easy way to compare which service is faster, more reliable or better value, so choosing one is difficult. That problem helped prompt the report," Wang Peng, a research fellow at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Saturday. CAICT report showed that model service prices rose sharply in 2026 both in China and overseas. After adjusting for different billing methods so prices can be compared, the average domestic price rose from 6.8 yuan ($1.02) in the second half of 2025 to 13.46 yuan this year - nearly double. Yet overseas prices remain far higher: typical models launched since 2026 average about 117.8 yuan on the same basis, roughly 8.7 times the domestic level. The supply side is also upgrading. On Saturday, Moonshot AI launched Kimi K3.1 Pro, a 3-trillion-parameter open-source model with a 1-million-token context window, which the company describes as the "world's largest open-source model by parameter count." "Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest closed-source models," Moonshot AI said. According to the company, it scored 65.7 percent on the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding-agent benchmark, above GPT-6 Astra's 58.2 percent and close to Claude Opus 5.5's 66.4 percent. According to media reports, Kimi K3.1 Pro's price is one-fifth that of GPT-6 Astra and about half of Claude Opus 5.5. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were the latest AI models released by OpenAI and Anthropic, respectively, in late September. Other Chinese vendors are pushing into more specialized and higher-value scenarios. Volcengine, ByteDance's cloud unit, began the first enterprise trials of its Seedance 2.5 4K video-generation model, supplying the model to 20 studios and directors, with the first titles expected to air as early as next month, the company said. And on Friday, at the 2026 World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference, a national AI application pilot base released what it called the industry's first automotive AI foundation. The base manages 112.7 EFLOPS (a unit of the speed of computer systems, meaning one quintillion floating-point operations per second) of computing power and has deployed six AI agents covering styling design, process planning, visual quality inspection, intelligent operations, autonomous-driving data generation and model training. From "burning cash to win customers" to "earning through service," the competitive logic of China's token market has changed, said Wang. "The simultaneous rise in prices and usage offers a blunt market judgment: customers are not paying more for more expensive tokens, but for models that solve more problems," Wang added.

item.title: Teodoro charges at China with a paper shield
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24 13:52:00
Philippines Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro Jr. delivers his speech during a plenary session of the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Shangri-la Dialogue Defense Summit in Singapore, 31 May 2026. Photo: VCG Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. has once again been huffing at China, claiming that if China were to remove the Philippine ship that is illegally "grounded" at China's Ren'ai Jiao, it would constitute a so-called "act of war." He also warned that if Chinese personnel boarded the vessel, it could trigger the US-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty. Yet no sooner had he made these threats than he began backpedaling, clarifying that an “act of war” does not necessarily mean the two countries would enter a “state of war,” as “only the President and Congress can declare war.” Teodoro is charging at China with a shield made of paper, only to retreat behind Marcos and the US before China has even made a move. This performance essentially lays bare his opportunism and cowardice. Teodoro's remarks were based on an unverified Philippine media report claiming that “China was considering 10 countermeasures against the Philippines,” including removing the grounded ship, blocking supplies, sanctioning Philippine politicians, reducing oil and fertilizer supplies, and restricting tourism. Teodoro admitted that he had not even read the report, yet he was already rushing to issue warnings. This suggests that he knows perfectly well the price of provoking China and that the Philippines cannot afford to pay it. For all his tough talk, he is effectively crying out in pain in anticipation of the consequences. China has indisputable sovereignty over Ren'ai Jiao and its adjacent waters. The China Coast Guard carries out law enforcement operations to safeguard rights in waters under its jurisdiction in accordance with the law. Its demand that the Philippines remove the illegally grounded warship is legitimate and well-founded. If the Philippines continues to gamble on provocations, persists in illegal intrusions and the reinforcement of structures at Ren'ai Jiao, or even attempts to forcibly break through China's law-enforcement controls, China will certainly take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests. The Philippines should harbor no illusions on this matter. The further it goes in provoking China, the heavier the blows it will suffer. By then, it will be too late to try to salvage the situation by hiding behind others. Last month, Philippine media reported on a letter allegedly signed by Teodoro and addressed to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) official. According to the reported contents, Teodoro pledged that if he were to assume presidential power in the future, he would continue strengthening the US-Philippines alliance and pursuing a hard-line policy toward China. He also reportedly planned to manufacture maritime friction at Ren'ai Jiao during an ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting to portray China as a country "bullying a smaller nation." The Philippine Department of National Defense promptly denied the letter's authenticity, saying it “is false and fake,” but provided no evidence. The authenticity of the letter remains to be verified. Nevertheless, the pattern of behavior described in it closely mirrors Teodoro's own conduct, lending further weight to the suspicion that Teodoro is "on a mission." He is attempting to manufacture friction to serve his personal political ambitions, using his hardline stance toward China as a token of allegiance to external forces. Before trying to intimidate China with cries of an "act of war," Teodoro had better think carefully about the consequences of his words. No external power will foot the bill for his reckless rhetoric, and any so-called "treaty" will become nothing more than a scrap of paper in the face of risks of this magnitude.

item.title: China issues guidelines to boost AI-driven job creation, mitigate employment displacement risks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23 19:10:00
Staff members conduct data collection for various scenarios at a company’s embodied?AI robot data collection and training center in Suqian, East China’s Jiangsu Province on September 3, 2026. Through real-robot simulation, on-site operations, and human-robot collaboration, the center precisely captures multi-dimensional core data such as vision, motion, and environment data, laying a solid data foundation for the optimization and iteration of embodied-AI models. Photo: VCG China has rolled out a set of policy measures to create more jobs through artificial intelligence (AI), improve employment quality and mitigate the impact of job displacement resulting from AI applications, helping build an employment-friendly development model, amid the rapid development and growing use of the technology. The guidelines, issued by the General Office of the State Council and made public on Friday, outline 18 major tasks across six areas, covering AI-driven job creation, employment-friendly AI adoption, workforce training, employment services, labor rights and social security protections, and employment risk monitoring and response. The document aims to strengthen AI's positive role in creating job opportunities, enhancing traditional jobs through AI, improving employment quality and stimulating entrepreneurship, while mitigating the impact of AI-related job displacement, according to the guidelines. It also seeks to promote inclusive development by ensuring that technological progress and industrial upgrading go hand in hand with employment growth and improvements in people's livelihoods. To strengthen AI's job creation potential, the guidelines call for expanding employment opportunities in emerging sectors, helping micro, small and medium-sized enterprises retain and expand their workforce, developing new AI-related employment and entrepreneurship models, and accelerating the development of new AI-related occupations. The document also calls for building an employment-friendly pathway for AI adoption, including tapping the employment potential of AI in traditional industries, easing job displacement pressures arising from AI applications and establishing mechanisms to assess employment risks associated with the technology. To improve workers' digital literacy and employability, the guidelines call for coordinated efforts to develop innovative AI talent and the implementation of dedicated AI training programs. In terms of employment services, the document calls for using AI to facilitate the implementation of employment policies, improve the intelligence and efficiency of employment services, and strengthen support for workers transitioning to new jobs or occupations. The guidelines also emphasize improving labor rights and social security systems to keep pace with technological changes. Measures include improving labor rights protections to accommodate human-AI collaboration, improving social security arrangements for flexible workers and those in new forms of employment, and refining income distribution mechanisms to adapt to AI development. To address potential employment risks arising from AI applications, the document proposes strengthening employment risk monitoring and early-warning systems related to AI applications, stepping up research into AI's impact on employment, and improving mechanisms to respond to emerging employment risks. The guidelines call on local governments and relevant departments to implement the measures in accordance with local conditions. Human resources and social security authorities and development and reform departments at all levels are also urged to strengthen coordination to ensure the measures are effectively implemented. The latest guidelines are in line with a five-year plan for implementing the employment-first strategy released by the State Council in June, which called for advancing the "AI Plus" initiative, fostering more entrepreneurial projects involving innovative AI applications and the commercialization of technological achievements, exploring new forms of work involving human-AI collaboration, and strengthening AI's role in job creation. item.title: 16 killed, 54 injured after 7.0-magnitude quake hits China's Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23 10:54:00
CHINA / SOCIETY 16 killed, 54 injured after 7.0-magnitude quake hits China's Xizang By Xinhua Published: Oct 23, 2026 10:54 AM
Sixteen people were killed and 54 others injured after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County of Nagqu City in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. Thursday. The regional disaster prevention, reduction and relief committee activated a Level III emergency response for natural disaster relief on Friday. The State Council earthquake relief headquarters and the Ministry of Emergency Management also upgraded the national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III. As of 7 a.m. Friday, 11 of the injured were in serious condition, while 43 sustained minor injuries. More than 330 houses collapsed or were damaged. The damage caused by the quake is being further evaluated, and disaster relief work is underway. More than 12,000 residents have been evacuated, according to the city's earthquake relief headquarters. Quake relief supplies allocated by the authorities at various levels have been arriving at the quake-hit zone as of early Friday morning, including 1,000 sets of prefabricated houses, more than 3,200 tents, over 2,800 folding beds, and other daily necessities like quilts, stoves and clothes. The area surrounding the epicenter has an average altitude of more than 4,800 meters. The temperatures there will be as low as minus nine degrees Celsius in the next three days, with intermittent snow expected Saturday in the three townships near the epicenter, according to local weather forecast authorities.

item.title: Ninety years on, the great Long March spirit is a light shining on the world: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23 00:36:00
Marching toward prosperity. Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The great Long March spirit has been deeply etched into the DNA of Chinese society. It is the determination to rise to challenges and to persist for the long haul; it is the courage to fear no sacrifice and to dare to try; it is the clarity to face reality and actively seek change; and above all, it is the original aspiration of standing with the people through life and death, sharing weal and woe, and striving arduously. The 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army was commemorated at a grand gathering in Beijing on Thursday morning. General Secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee Xi Jinping, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, attended the gathering and delivered an important speech. Xi stressed that the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. As an important part of the spiritual lineage of the CPC, it transcends time and space and remains evergreen. It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously. The Long March was a beam of light that burst forth from the Chinese nation at its darkest hour. It showed the world clearly that, even in an old China mired in darkness with no visible way out, there was a group of people striving with all their might to build a new China. In the book The Life Millennium: The 100 Most Important Events and People of the Past 1000 Years, published by the American Time-Life Books, scholars from around the world jointly selected 100 events that shaped the world from 1000 to 2000 AD. The Long March of the Red Army was one of three historical events from China to make the list. It profoundly inspires people that as long as one remains firm in will and unyielding in the face of setbacks, a way out can always be found through continuous exploration, and an entirely new path can be opened. From Edgar Snow to Henry Kissinger, from Nelson Mandela to Fidel Castro, many observers and strategists have pondered why this Long March in the East was able to succeed. To this day, whenever China astonishes the world with technological breakthroughs or reshapes perceptions with development miracles, the world still asks: "How do the Chinese do it?" These questions all point to the same answer: We have found the right path - a path of never yielding, always moving forward, and never retreating. The Long March is both a spiritual treasure that inspires the Chinese people and a display of the Chinese nation's resilient character to the world. Today, the term "Long March" has become a shared name for any arduous journey that ultimately reaches its destination. In this sense, the value of the Long March lies not only in the arrival itself, but in the act of continuing to set forth, again and again. After the victory of the Long March, the nation did not stop: It kept marching through the flames of the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, kept advancing on the tide of reform and opening-up, and continues to advance under the call of the new era, all the way toward the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Today, the great Long March spirit has been deeply etched into the DNA of Chinese society. It is the determination to rise to challenges and to persist for the long haul; it is the courage to fear no sacrifice and to dare to try; it is the clarity to face reality and actively seek change; and above all, it is the original aspiration of standing with the people through life and death, sharing weal and woe, and striving arduously. Ninety years on, the great Long March spirit no longer belongs only to history; it is a light that grows ever brighter and shines upon the world. Currently, global governance is experiencing a "darkest hour": climate change, the North-South divide, geopolitical conflicts, and the undercurrents of deglobalization. Old paradigms are failing, and new rules have yet to take shape. Solving many major issues requires long-term planning and sustained effort that transcend political cycles and short-term gains and losses. The spirit of firm conviction, unity and cooperation, and unyielding struggle transcends national borders and ideologies. It inspires humanity to overcome adversity and pursue a brighter future. This both suggests that global governance needs to blaze new trails toward common development, common security, and common prosperity, and helps the world better understand the spiritual bedrock of the Chinese nation, enabling outsiders to better grasp where this "enabling great power" is heading. "Where the spirit lies, there lies the strength." The great Long March spirit resonates with the Chinese nation's cultural tradition of constant self-improvement and has gained new contemporary meaning in the process of Chinese modernization. While it is no longer possible for China today to replicate the march back then, this spirit will always remain, proving to the world that the Chinese nation possesses extraordinary resilience. After decades of struggle, China has long since become the world's second-largest economy and is comprehensively advancing the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The enduring national resilience behind the great Long March spirit has been a key factor in creating this development miracle. It is the confidence that allows China to navigate storms and seize the historical initiative, and it also provides a stabilizing expectation for a world full of uncertainty. In the 1980s, Zbigniew Brzezinski, who once served as US national security advisor, walked with his family along the route once taken by the Red Army. He later reflected: "The Long March is more than an epic of almost unmatched heroism." Today, more and more foreigners are coming to China to retrace the Long March route, and places like Loushan Pass have once again become a popular destination for visitors. This is one indication that the great Long March spirit is increasingly needed by the world. As a spiritual monument that the Chinese nation has offered to the world, its importance will become even more prominent in the future. As military writer Wang Shuzeng once described: "The Long March belongs to that category of events in human history which, even after the passage of long years, continue to be sought after by people." "The history of the Long March has never faded; the road of the Long March continues to extend." For China, on the new journey, the Long March has no endpoint. To carry forward the great Long March spirit is to always maintain a high-spirited posture of storming passes and seizing fortresses, to continue the arduous trek on the journey of Chinese modernization, and to respond to all risks and challenges with an unstoppable fighting spirit. It is to both successfully navigate the Long March of our own generation and infuse a world marked by turbulence and transformation with confidence and strength from the East.

item.title: GT Voice：What does Japan get in return for investing in US chip plants?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 22:19:00
An AI-generated image of a chip Photo: VCG While Japan is in the midst of a major push to revive its chip sector, it is being pressed to build America's, Reuters reported on Tuesday. The report comes after news that Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries. It is part of a pledge to invest $550 billion in the US made with the Trump administration in return for lower tariffs. While the investment appears to be a deepening of the US-Japan alliance, it is actually a costly drain on Japan's reboot of its semiconductor sector. Some may believe that investment in the US and domestic investment can be compatible, and they will both benefit Japanese equipment manufacturers. But the bilateral agreement reached in 2025 already showed that the US is the side that could benefit significantly from Japan's investment. Japan's investment projects will be selected and managed by the US, and cash flows generated by the investments are to be split equally until Japan recoups its "deemed allocation amount," after which 90 percent of the cash flow will go to the US. This arrangement means Japan is putting up its capital to build up America's domestic chip production capacity, only to end up with meager returns. Some have already pointed out that this kind of investment is essentially a "tax" in exchange for lower tariffs for Japanese exports to the US. This is the core reality that should not be overlooked: in Washington's calculation, the industrial capabilities of its allies are resources to be mobilized and made to bear the costs of America's own industrial priorities. The so-called "Chip Alliance" - publicly framed as a collective effort to safeguard global supply chain security - is in essence a mechanism that pulls the fiscal resources of US allies directly into Washington's industrial policy toolbox. The allies pay the bills, the US builds the factories, and the production capacity and decision-making power remain in American hands. Japan has long imagined that it is deepening its alliance and guaranteeing its own security, but in reality it is subsidizing America's manufacturing reshoring campaign. To be fair, the GlobalFoundries deal alone does not prove that Japan's semiconductor revival will fail. Japan has not abandoned its domestic semiconductor ambitions, with projects including its flagship chip-sector project Rapidus still moving forward. The Japanese government pledges to roll out subsidies to support local advanced process research and development. The crux of the problem, however, is whether Japan's fiscal situation can possibly bear the burden of both massive US-bound investment and its own domestic semiconductor revival at the same time. Japan's government debt-to-GDP ratio ranks the highest among all developed economies. The Takaichi government has ambitions to pour public-private investment totaling some $2.3 trillion through fiscal 2040 across 17 strategic Japanese sectors, including artificial intelligence and chips. The $550 billion investment commitment in the US is no small sum either. As more resources are funneled into American investment, how much is left for domestic plans becomes a real constraint. Investing in the US and reviving capabilities at home are not mutually exclusive, but whether Japan's finances can sustain both is an open question. Japan once sought to leverage the US-Japan alliance and draw on American supply chain resources to nurture its own domestic semiconductor capacity, with the ultimate aim of reviving its chip industry. But the GlobalFoundries project has laid bare the flaw in that thinking. The more Japan pours into the US, the more fragile its domestic semiconductor industry becomes, and the more its place in the global chip chain is locked into that of a supporting supplier to American industry. If Japan cannot wake up from the illusion that clinging to the US can revive its industry, the only outcome waiting for it is the wholesale hollowing out of its domestic semiconductor industry.

item.title: Ukraine's awkward position: Dependent on the US, powerless to push back
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 21:22:00
Ukraine Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Tension between the US and Ukraine has once again erupted into the open. Recent remarks by US Vice President JD Vance have laid bare a long-standing yet often obscured reality in US-Ukraine relations: Ukraine is not a formal US ally, and Washington does not want it to join NATO. Vance also called on Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy facilities. His comments appear to mark a clear boundary of US interests underpinning its Ukraine policy. The US may support Ukraine, but that does not mean it will underwrite every demand Kiev makes. Ukraine can rely on American aid, but it cannot expect Washington to stand unconditionally on its side. Vance has not articulated a brand-new policy. His statement is a public restatement of the current US administration's consistent position. The previous US administration, by contrast, stressed the moral imperative of supporting Ukraine, tying Ukrainian security closely to European security and US credibility, fostering a political relationship that resembled an alliance - despite the fact that Ukraine is not a NATO member, nor does it have a mutual defense treaty with the US. That it is not a formal ally has always been true. What stands out now is that the US no longer blurs this line deliberately, but proactively spells it out publicly. "Ukraine is trapped in an awkward, painful position. It cannot do without US assistance, yet it holds no leverage over Washington," Zhang Hong, a research fellow at the Institute of Russian, Eastern European and Central Asian Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. Why is the US choosing this moment to publicly reaffirm this status? The answer lies in Vance's other demand: "Ukraine should stop attacking Russian energy facilities." An earlier diesel fuel deal struck between the US and Russia had already opened rifts in US-Ukraine relations. Compared with Ukraine's battlefield priorities, the US prioritizes its own energy market positioning and domestic political pressures. Compounding this, Washington has delayed deliveries of a batch of weapons to Ukraine. By partially cutting the aid pipeline while explicitly defining the bilateral relationship as non-allied, the US is essentially creating diplomatic cover to ratchet up pressure on Kiev. Should Ukraine's military actions run counter to core US interests, Washington can potentially scale back support and recalibrate its policy, laying full blame for escalation at Kiev's door. Aid is a discretionary favor, while rolling back support is seen as a legitimate policy choice - this has become the underlying logic of the US' Ukraine strategy. This does not mean Ukraine has lost its strategic value to the US. "In the European theater, the Ukraine crisis remains a key instrument for the US to sustain transatlantic security bonds. The US, in turn, retains sway over Europe's security agenda and reaps economic gains from defense industrial cooperation," Zhang explained. Toward Russia, the Ukraine crisis also serves as a vital topic for US diplomatic maneuvering. Whether negotiating ceasefire terms, security consultations or potential future energy and economic accords, Washington keeps the Ukraine crisis alive to preserve room for bargaining with Moscow, he added. Washington's support for Ukraine has never been an open-ended, unconditional moral obligation, but a strategic choice weighed rigorously against costs and benefits. Clearly, Ukraine's interests and grievances are never Washington's priority. Even when it comes to making the kind of deals Washington wants, Ukraine lacks the leverage to deliver. Ukraine's mineral resources available for potential deals are valued at around $500 billion, while potential joint projects between the US and Russia are worth as much as $14 trillion. By comparison, Ukraine's bargaining power is overwhelmingly outmatched. Ukraine has tried to tie itself to Europe, hoping European leaders would lobby Washington to sustain aid. Yet Europe maintains its own interest calculations, and the support it can offer Kiev is steadily dwindling. This leaves Ukraine stuck in a dilemma. The US is deliberately decoupling its own interests from Ukraine's aspirations. It has no objection to continuing to use the Ukraine issue to pressure Russia, yet refuses to assume treaty obligations for Ukraine's security goals. Partnership continues when Kiev's military moves align with Washington's objectives; when interests collide, Ukraine's demands are the ones usually sacrificed. From the moment Washington clarified the boundaries of US-Ukraine relations, one truth emerges: Ukraine has always been a geopolitical tool for the US, never its core interest. This unequal dynamic of dependence and limited bargaining power has left Ukraine in an awkward and passive position from the start.
